cues.text: Repeated prompts become messy when useful instructions are mixed with changing details. I’ll show you how to separate them.
You’ll build one reusable prompt.
This isn’t a magical prompt for every task. It’s a practical template with labelled spaces for the audience, source, constraints
and required result.
A clear request describes the goal, context, input, constraints, and output.
We’ll decide which parts stay fixed and which become labelled fields.
This one-off request asks for a friendly announcement for local residents. It requires a heading, two short paragraphs, preserved details
and no guessing. The source notes contain the event name, date, time, location, registration rule, and contact method.
To reuse the request, we must expose the values that could change.
I’ll split the request into fixed instructions and changing values. The fixed instructions define the recurring job: rewrite supplied notes, preserve facts, avoid unsupported additions
and follow the required structure. Details such as audience, purpose, source, constraints
and format belong in labelled fields because they change with each use.
I’ll use seven clear fields. Task defines the work; Audience and Purpose identify who the result serves and why.
Source Text contains the material. Must Preserve protects essential details. Constraints set limits
while Output Format defines the finished shape. One fixed rule says to use only the source and flag missing information instead of inventing it.
Square brackets are readable labels, not universal commands. Braces, blank lines, or a table could work too.
What matters is that each field clearly shows where a new value belongs. Keep the labels consistent
then replace only their values whenever you reuse the template.
Keep instructions separate from source material. Instructions define the task; the source provides the permitted material.
A heading and divider make that boundary visible. Use material you created, own, have permission to process, or may otherwise use
and remove unnecessary private information. The source supports the draft doesn’t verify itself.
A reusable prompt needs a rule for incomplete inputs. If the location field is empty, don’t let the assistant guess. Write
“If a required field is empty, identify it and do not complete the task.” The useful response is, “Missing: location.”
You can then find the information, ask the responsible person, or finish manually without hiding uncertainty.
The template also needs a review checklist. Does the draft perform the task, preserve names, dates, numbers, and commitments
and avoid unsupported details? Does it match the requested length and format, while showing assumptions or missing information?
Compare the draft with your source. This checklist isn’t proof, and consequential claims still require suitable independent evidence.
I’ll test the template with fictional source notes. The Green Corner Workshop invites local residents to the Community Room on 18th November 2026
from 14:00 to 15:30. Registration through the event form is required. Before submitting, I confirm the complete date, time range
venue, and registration instruction. These are source notes, not a generated answer.
I fill the fields without changing the stable instructions. The task is to rewrite the notes as an announcement for local residents.
The source field contains the exact notes. Must Preserve lists the event name, date, time, location, registration requirement, and contact method.
The constraints forbid unsupported details, while the output format requires one heading and two short paragraphs.
The generated draft says: “Green Corner Workshop. Join local residents for the Green Corner Workshop on 18th November 2026, from 14:00 to 15:30
in the Community Room. Registration is required. Please use the event form to register.”
I label it as generated material, place it beside the source notes, and begin five checks.
Check one passes because the draft is the requested announcement. For check two, I compare every protected detail with the source notes.
The event name, date, year, times, Community Room location, registration requirement, and event form all match.
I inspect the material directly rather than asking the assistant to judge its own accuracy.
For check three, I confirm that the draft adds no price, organizer, guarantee, extra activity, or registration deadline.
Check four passes because it has one heading and two short paragraphs. For check five, no field is missing
and no assumption appears as fact. This only proves that the fictional draft reflects the fictional notes,
not that the event exists or remains current.
Suppose the draft said, “Free refreshments will be provided in the Main Hall.”
That fails because the source names the Community Room and says nothing about refreshments. I would remove the unsupported promise and restore the correct location.
If I couldn’t repair it confidently, I’d write directly from the source notes, using the completed fields as my brief. Reuse should reduce effort
never make errors harder to challenge.
After the successful run, I return to the blank master. Its fields are empty, but the instructions and checklist remain.
Save it in a notes or document app with a task-based name, such as “Rewrite notes as a short announcement.”
Keep each completed copy separate so old details don’t enter a new prompt.
The second fictional case tests adaptability. The Riverside Book Swap is for students and staff at the Library Entrance on 3rd December 2026,
from 12:30 to 14:00. The reminder asks each person to bring up to three clean, readable books.
Questions go to the information desk. The task stays the same, but the case-specific values change.
I replace only the fields: audience, purpose, and source notes. Must Preserve lists the Riverside Book Swap name, date, time, location
three-book limit, condition requirement, and information desk. The constraints, output format, no-guessing rule, and checklist remain fixed.
Reusing the template saves effort while keeping every choice visible.
The second draft announces the Riverside Book Swap to students and staff on 3rd December 2026, from 12:30 to 14:00, at the Library Entrance.
It asks them to bring up to three clean, readable books and directs questions to the information desk. Those details and the requested structure match the source
with no unsupported fee, promise, organizer, or activity.
This comparison shows the method. Stable instructions govern the recurring job, labelled fields hold changing details, and the checklist defines success.
Add repeatedly missing fields to the template, but keep case-specific rules in that case’s constraints.
This prevents old details from becoming permanent instructions.
Use the template with any general assistant, or complete it in a notes app, document, or printed sheet. If no assistant is available
the filled template remains a clear writing brief for a person.
Generated wording isn’t evidence. Check important names, dates, numbers, permissions, and commitments against the original material or suitable independent evidence.
An assistant’s self-review may reveal problems, but it isn’t independent verification.
Your prompt is reusable when you can replace the labelled values without rewriting the stable instructions.
Use the checklist to compare each result with its source. In Lesson 31, we’ll separate instructions from source material more deliberately.
and I hope this lesson helps you turn a useful, one-off request into a prompt you can reuse.
Thank You for watching. I am EMMANUEL CORELS. See you in the next video.
